How to SAVE SOUTH AFRICA - AN INTERVIEW WITH MOELETSI MBEKI

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
IS SOUTH AFRICA IN NEED OF SAVING. MOELETSI MBEKI THINKS IT IS - WHAT IS WRONG AND HOW CAN IT BE FIXED?

Unique Selling Point:
MOELETSI MBEKI IS A WORLD RENOWNED AND RESPECTED ANALYST AND MAKES GREAT TV

Summary:
WHAT HAS GONE WRONG WITH SOUTH AFRICA - AND WHAT NEEDS TO HAPPEN TO FIX IT. MOELETSI MBEKI GIVES US HIS PERSPECTIVE

Further information:
HOW TO SAVE SOUTH AFRICA – MOELETSI AND NOBANTU MBEKI

In their new book How to Save South Africa Moeletsi Mbeki and his co author Nobantu Mbeki, pull no punches. They say South Africa is gridlocked and nothing has changed in South Africa for 350 years.

“There is something very very wrong with South Africa. And when we say something is wrong with South Africa, there is something very wrong with how the political elite are managing South Africa.”

Mbeki breaks South Africa down into five social groups: the economic elite, the political elite, blue collar workers; the underclass/ unemployed and the independent professionals/ NPO’ and new entrepreneurs.

Each social group comes in for examination. They describe the opaque nature of the relationship between capital, the state and the elite and declare that the consistent eruption of localized conflict increasing in scale and severity signals the obsolescence of the current order.

“ The state is failing to resolve conflicts, it is no longer an independent mediator as it has partnerships with labour and covert relationships with capital that are mediated by the elite.”

South Africa is a stunted capitalist society because its economy is unable to absorb nearly half its working age population and the society we most resemble today is Ancient Rome, where large numbers of people known as plebeians didn’t work. This underclass, created by the early British Mining magnates has an existence outside of the national economy.
Once they survived on remittances now they survive on grants as the mining industry declined and the welfare state emerged.

Our manufacturing industry is dying, mining is in decline, and as a middle income country we are a good example of one that is sinking steadily under the weight of globalization.
We have become riskier and face another probable ratings downgrade. To back their arguments they have spent many hours looking at the statistics. For example: the capitalist class has found ways of defending itself – one way is to move capital out and capital flight has risen from 9.3% in 1994 to a staggering 20% in 2007.

There are no sacred cows in the book and BEE also comes under fire: “ Investing in the elite has been the most unproductive and costly decision large firms historically operating in the South African market have made to date”

Mbeki argues that the face- off between the underclass and the current ruling elite has arrived and there really is no non- violent alternative as long as the social structure of South Africa remains broadly as it has, for centuries. In the book they explore four scenarios going forward. But ultimately their solution to save South Africa is for the underclass to control the state albeit in coalition with sections of the various social classes as they outline in the book. But right now there is a deadlock and the government has started to prepare for the inevitable showdown.

These preparations include:
• Militarization of the police
• Preparations for the suppression of freedom of the media
• Manipulation of judicial processes and personnel
• Purges of party members who propose alternative policies
• Refusal to introduce a constituency based electoral system to complement proportional representation
• Strengthening the powers of chiefs over the rural population

The reason for the deadlock is that unlike former elites, the African Nationalists are neither able nor willing to hand over control to the next administration. This is because the control of the state and its revenues is the means of sustenance of the current elite.


Effectively they say South Africa is a society with a hidden civil war and they link all forms of violence in the country to current economic activity in South Africa.

In a one on one with Bongani Bingwa we unpack this blunt prescription for our country’s future

Press Release:


How to Save South Africa
From an economy forecast at 0.4 percent growth to angry students, political turmoil, and around 11-million South Africans with little or no chance of ever working, how do we save South Africa? Carte Blanche sits down with political economist Moeletsi Mbeki who shares his blunt manifesto
for social change.


Script:


MOELETSI MBEKI AND HOW TO SAVE SOUTH AFRICA FINAL SCRIPT SEPTEMBER 2016

Commentary One
This week the ratings agencies touched down in SA.

Up sound plane lands

Here they will find an economy forecast at 0% growth

BANG! BANG!

Angry students, political turmoil, and around 11 million South Africans with little or no chance of ever working. So how do we save South Africa, asks Moeletsi and Nobantu Mbeki in their new book A Manifesto for social Change.

Moeletsi
We asked ourselves what other country has this huge population that is not working at all. The only other society that we found was ancient Rome which had the Plebeians which were given free bread and circus to keep them entertained. South Africa is another bread and circus society, it’s just that Bafana Bafana are not very good at creating the circus.

Commentary Two
More than two decades since 1994 Mbeki says South Africa is retreating further and further from the vision of a modern peaceful state, and that almost all the hallmarks associated with the old repressive white minority regime seem to remain in place

Moeletsi
First we should have completely overhauled our education system/ so we should have invested in our population instead of continuing to invest in the top elite of our society

Commentary Three
He says the IMF were recently shocked at how well our elites live

Moeletsi
They have this hugely comfortable environment luxury cars, lot of money and massive houses that is why we cannot fund free higher education – I got my higher education for free why because the British knew so it suppressed the consumption of the elite in order to fund the education of the masses

Bongani Link
Mbeki argues that the face-off between underclass and the current ruling elite has arrived and that there is really no non- violent alternative as long as the current social structure remains broadly has it has for centuries




Commentary Four
South African society has five distinct classes, he says: The political elite; the economic elite; blue collar workers; independent professionals &NGO’s and finally the underclass locked out of any meaningful economic activity

Moeletsi
There is a competition between the underclass and the political elite between ….the underclass is now realizing that without economic growth they will remain an underclass in perpetuity

Bongani
How do we awaken the underclass?
Mbeki
When SA was about to explode in the mid 1980’s what the Chairman of ANGLO AMERICAN a gentleman called Gavin Relly did, he said, we will not allow our country to blow up, I have to meet the ANC in exile. PW threatened to shoot down the plane he uses, he went anyway, now the business community is faced with the same situation, we need to go to the underclass and say we need a new coalition and this is what it will do for you

Bongani
How does business do that? Constantly we are told of the stranglehold of white monopoly capital. How do the same people go to the underclass and say we are your friends?

Moeletsi
This is all nonsense! There is no stranglehold of white monopoly capital over South Africa we have a stranglehold ironically of the parastatals, of Transnet – the state today is through enormous inefficiency of running the ports and railways
Bongani
You could say the same about Eskom and SAA
Moeletsi
…the notion that its a stranglehold of white monopoly capital is rubbish

Commentary Five
He adds covert relationships have developed between the political and economic elites and we are seeing an ANC increasingly at war with the black poor, who form the backbone of its electorate.

Moeletsi
Since the 17th century this violence by the state against the people is a key characteristic of how SA operates

Marikana shooting

Moeletsi
We saw in a most graphic way the shooting of the platinum miners by the police


Commentary Six
And service delivery protests have rocketed to around 14 thousand per year

Gun shot up sound

a hidden civil war suggests Mbeki, and a ticking time bomb.

Moeletsi
if you are going to have 14 000 incidents of essentially an uprising by the poor then you have to prepare for it– and the government is preparing by the way it is structuring the police and the intelligence they are going to be at the frontline between the political elite and the underclass

Bongani
What happens if we don’t get this right?
Moeletsi
If we don’t get this right what will happen is what happened to ancient Rome. You get an implosion.

Commentary seven
Government has started preparing for the inevitable showdown says Mbeki. We are seeing the militarization of the police, preparations to suppress media freedom, manipulation of judicial processes and personnel, purging of party members who propose alternative policies and strengthening the powers of the chiefs over the rural population

Bongani
Many people seem to think that if you were to recall president Zuma some of this would be resolved?
Mbeki
I don’t think so, these are systemic issues anyway the notion of recall is nonsense, according to our constitution there are only two ways to remove a president and that is through parliament not through political parties/ it was not constitutional when it was used against Thabo Mbeki, it wont be if its against Zuma and there have been impeachment votes that have failed because the ANC has the majority

Commentary eight
Recently bewildered South Africans have witnessed the ruling party itself imploding.

Up sound
Hoes! Hoes! Hoes!

Bongani
When you say people are obsessing about the ANC what do you mean

Moeletsi
We have a long history of independence of Africa and the parties that ended colonialism where are they today? Where is Nkrumah party where is Kenyatta –banda – nowhere, where is Kaunda nowhere – where is ZANU PF? Nowhere – kept there by the army but it uses violence to stay in power – so why do we think that the ANC will rule till the second coming of Jesus Christ. It’s not going to!

THE END 8 minutes

Out at 00 09 00 00

Moeletsi Mbeki on how capital needs a new coalition with the underclass
Moeletsi
We need a new coalition whose primary interest is the growth of the economy.

PROMO TWO 15 seconder

Commentary
Moeletsi Mbeki’s manifesto for Social Change and how we can Save South Africa

Commentary

Moeletsi
If we don’t get this right what will happen is what happened to ancient Rome. You get an implosion.
